briefing.text: There is no ready-made 'clinically actionable' variable in this study's tables. The library's read of the files found that data_mutations.txt carries only a Hotspot flag and that none of the mutation, CNA, SV or clinical sample files has an ONCOGENIC, HIGHEST_LEVEL or other OncoKB-style column. Confirm this yourself from the column lists. What the files do hold are the inputs a knowledgebase uses to assign an actionability level: gene, protein change (HGVSp_Short), Variant_Classification, discrete CNA call, fusion partners in data_sv.txt, and tumour type (ONCOTREE_CODE, CANCER_TYPE). Any actionable fraction therefore depends on a rule set you build. Write down an explicit gene x alteration x tumour-type rule table (OncoKB-style standard-care levels 1-2, optionally level 3), apply it per sample, state it in your reasoning, and decide deliberately whether a fraction resting on your own rule table is firm enough to support or contradict a point claim.
briefing.reason: The central variable of the hypothesis is not a column in the data; how the team handles that determines both the method and which label is defensible.

briefing.text: The fraction of samples called 'actionable' swings several-fold with the evidence-level cutoff, the knowledgebase date and who annotates. Re-annotating the same 47,271 tumours gave 8.9% (2017 OncoKB) versus 31.6% (2022 OncoKB) at level 1-2. The 2017 OncoKB abstract reads, as written and with nested wording: 'Forty-one percent of samples harbored at least one potentially actionable alteration, of which 7.5% were predictive of clinical benefit from a standard treatment'. Two annotation services agreed only moderately on level-1 actionability (kappa 0.44; 27 gene-variant-diagnosis combinations called by both, 58 by one alone, 6 by the other alone). 'Oncogenic/driver' is not 'actionable': TP53, CDKN2A and most KRAS alterations are frequent drivers with little or no actionability. So a hand-built rule table is one opinion, not a measurement. Compute the fraction under several named definitions: (a) strict standard-care only (FDA-label or guideline biomarker in that tumour type), (b) plus investigational level 3, (c) permissive: plus off-tumour-type (3B), biological-evidence level 4 and resistance markers. List the genes contributing most hits under each and confirm none of the count comes from TP53/CDKN2A/non-G12C-KRAS style drivers. Never report one number without naming its definition; prefer the definition that fits the era of the samples (panel versions indicate the era); if strict and permissive definitions fall on opposite sides of 20%, say that the verdict rests on the definition and choose the label on that basis.
briefing.reason: A single self-chosen definition can land almost anywhere relative to 20%; the team needs to bracket the estimate with strict and permissive definitions before judging the claim.

briefing.text: Counting any mutation in an 'actionable gene' overstates actionability; only specific alterations qualify. Examples: EGFR L858R, exon 19 deletions, exon 20 insertions and T790M, not any EGFR missense; KRAS G12C, not G12D/G12V; BRAF V600E; MET exon 14 skipping splice/deletion variants or MET amplification; truncating or known deleterious BRCA1/2; kinase fusions of ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK1-3, FGFR2/3; ERBB2 amplification. Variants of unknown significance and silent/intronic calls are not actionable. Filter mutations on HGVSp_Short, Variant_Classification and the Hotspot flag; in data_cna.txt use only +2 (amplification) and -2 (deep deletion); in data_sv.txt read the event description/annotation and both gene symbols to confirm a real fusion of the right gene rather than any rearrangement or intragenic event. Use the variant-level count as primary and report the gene-level count only as an upper bound.
briefing.reason: A gene-level shortcut is the easiest way to build the rule table and it inflates the numerator, which can move the estimate across 20%.

briefing.text: Actionability is tumour-type specific, so a gene-only or variant-only list misclassifies: the same alteration is standard-care in one cancer and only off-label/investigational in another (e.g. BRAF V600E in melanoma vs other sites, KRAS G12C in lung, ERBB2 amplification in breast/gastric, PIK3CA in breast, IDH1 and FGFR2 fusions in cholangiocarcinoma, FGFR3 in bladder, BRCA1/2 in prostate/breast/pancreas/ovary). This cohort is mixed: mostly non-small cell lung cancer, then prostate, bladder, pancreatic, hepatobiliary, breast and many small groups, with some samples having cancer type NA or unknown primary. Join every alteration to the sample's ONCOTREE_CODE / CANCER_TYPE before assigning a level, keep in-tumour-type and off-tumour-type hits as separate tiers and report both, and tabulate the actionable fraction by cancer type to see whether lung drives the pooled figure.
briefing.reason: Whether off-tumour-type hits are counted changes the numerator, and the cohort is a mix of cancer types, so the rule table must be applied per tumour type.

briefing.text: The hypothesis denominator is 'samples with somatic alterations', not all samples. In these cBioPortal-format files a sample with no mutation simply has no rows in data_mutations.txt (it was still profiled), and a sample can be altered only through a copy-number change or a structural variant. data_clinical_sample.txt has 1,446 samples. Build three sample sets (>=1 row in mutations, >=1 gene at +2/-2 in CNA, >=1 row in SV), take their union as 'samples with somatic alterations', and compare its size with the profiled samples in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt / data_clinical_sample.txt. Use the union as the denominator for the hypothesis as worded, give actionable/all-profiled beside it as a sensitivity check, and flag it if the two give different verdicts. In data_cna.txt, NA means 'not profiled for copy number', not 'no alteration': the matrix has a column for all 1,446 samples but whole blocks of sample columns are NA. Count NA genes per sample and cross-tabulate against GENE_PANEL and the cna column of the gene panel matrix. Treat those samples as unassessed for CNA (they can still be altered or actionable through mutations or SVs), never as CNA-negative, and state that amplification-based actionability (ERBB2, MET) is under-ascertained in them.
briefing.reason: The denominator named in the hypothesis has to be constructed across three alteration tables, and mishandling absent rows or NA copy-number calls changes both numerator and denominator.

briefing.text: The study mixes two very different assays in one sample table, often from the same patients: 800 samples on the 129-gene plasma cell-free DNA panel (GENE_PANEL ACCESS129, Sample Type often 'Unknown') and 646 on tissue tumour panels (IMPACT468 574, IMPACT410 39, IMPACT505 26, IMPACT341 7). The plasma panel covers fewer genes and plasma has lower sensitivity for fusions and copy-number changes. Plasma samples are also often uninformative: low tumour shedding gives false negatives (sensitivity for tissue-confirmed drivers 58-86% overall, near 100% only at tumour fraction >=10%), so many plasma samples have zero detected alterations and those with alterations are enriched for high-shedding, advanced disease; conditioning on 'samples with alterations' therefore gives a higher actionable fraction than dividing by all plasma samples. A claim about 'the samples' may refer to only one assay. Tabulate GENE_PANEL; compute the altered-sample denominator and the actionable fraction separately for ACCESS129, for IMPACT and pooled; count plasma samples with zero alterations of any type and do not read them as true negatives. Report all three strata; if the verdict differs by stratum, state which stratum you take as the study's subject and why rather than silently pooling.
briefing.reason: Which samples the claim is about (plasma, tissue or both) is ambiguous and the fraction can differ by assay, so the team must stratify before choosing the figure to judge against 20%.

briefing.text: A point claim ('20%') cannot be judged by eye. Published sentences of this type are often nested ('X% had an alteration, of which Y% were actionable'), so the same data give different percentages for different denominators, and with about 1,000 samples a binomial interval is only about +/-2.5 points, so 20% is easily excluded by a rule set slightly too wide or too narrow. Fix in advance what counts as agreement (e.g. the estimate rounds to about 20%, or its interval covers 20%), then compute the estimate and an interval for each defensible definition and denominator. Tumour-agnostic biomarkers held in the clinical table rather than the alteration tables (MSI_TYPE unstable, high TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS) can move the count: run with and without them. Samples are not independent: the 1,446 samples come from about 617 patients (several plasma and tissue samples per patient), so a patient with many serial samples and a persistent driver is counted repeatedly and a naive binomial interval is too narrow. Keep the sample-level fraction as primary because the claim says 'samples', show a patient-level figure beside it (patient actionable if any altered sample is; also first-sample-only), and judge 20% against a cluster-aware interval (bootstrap resampling patients, or a cluster-adjusted Wilson interval). If every defensible definition lands far from 20% the claim is contradicted; if only some reach 20%, report that the verdict is definition-dependent and name the definition you rely on.
briefing.reason: The team needs a pre-set agreement criterion and an honest interval; repeated samples per patient and tumour-agnostic markers both affect whether an estimate can be told apart from 20%.

briefing.text: Not every listed variant is a tumour-derived somatic alteration. In plasma, clonal haematopoiesis (DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, PPM1D, also TP53, ATM, CHEK2) and germline variants are common false 'somatic' calls unless a matched white-blood-cell normal was used, and a few samples here are flagged SOMATIC_STATUS 'Unmatched'. Germline BRCA1/2, ATM or CHEK2 would wrongly add to 'somatic actionable'. Tabulate Mutation_Status in data_mutations.txt, SV_Status in data_sv.txt and SOMATIC_STATUS in the sample table; count how many actionable calls rest on ATM/CHEK2/BRCA or on unmatched samples. Keep only somatic calls, rerun excluding unmatched samples, and treat DNA-repair-gene hits in plasma as a sensitivity tier rather than core actionable.
briefing.reason: The hypothesis is about somatic alterations; non-somatic calls in DNA-repair genes could add to both the altered and the actionable counts, so the team should check how much of the figure rests on them.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed that a hand-built gene x variant x tumour-type rule table, written from general knowledge with no reference annotation to check it against, is close enough to a knowledgebase annotation to contradict a point claim. Neither validated its table against anything external, and the two tables disagree: on essentially the same altered plasma samples (595 vs 596) the strict tiers differ by about 60 samples (roughly ten percentage points). Neither team knows which rules cause the gap.

Both teams assumed that today's standard-of-care biomarker list is the right definition of 'clinically actionable'. Neither computed a tier restricted to what was standard of care when the samples were sequenced (the panel versions date the samples), although several rules that carry weight in a lung-dominated cohort are recent approvals.

Both teams treated all 800 plasma samples as one homogeneous population (apart from patient clustering and cancer type). Neither asked whether the plasma samples fall into sub-cohorts (e.g. first vs serial on-treatment draws, patients with vs without a tissue sample) with different actionable fractions.

Both teams read '20%' as a point value to be compared with their range and chose 'False' because every tier lies above it; neither wrote down a tolerance for the narrowest defensible tier, and neither gave a cluster confidence interval for its narrowest stress test.

Both teams assumed every released plasma call (including structural-variant rows and calls at very low allele fraction) counts equally toward numerator and denominator; team A classified SV rows from the Event_Info text only.
unused_evidence: Patient pairing of plasma and tissue: all 449 patients with a tissue sample also have plasma (617 plasma patients). Neither team used the tissue sample of the same patient to check whether the plasma calls its strict tier relies on are confirmed in tissue, or whether actionability differs between plasma samples with and without a paired tissue sample.

Columns that split the 800 plasma samples and were not used: SAMPLE_TYPE (Unknown 525 / Primary 156 / Metastasis 118 / Local Recurrence 1), TUMOR_PURITY (blank 582 / 'default' 216 / '0' 2), SAMPLE_COVERAGE, and the per-patient sample order in the sample ID (506 patients have one plasma sample, 111 have 2-14).

Structural-variant detail columns in data_sv.txt (Site1/Site2 gene, region, Site2_Effect_On_Frame, Class, Connection_Type, Annotation). Plasma has 72 SV rows in 70 samples and many are labelled intergenic, 'Antisense Fusion' or 'Deletion of N exons'; these columns say whether a rearrangement is an in-frame kinase fusion.

t_alt_count / t_ref_count in data_mutations.txt are filled for every plasma row (median allele fraction about 1.6%, 5% of calls at about 0.1%). The library advised against adding a VAF filter; neither team reported the with/without sensitivity figure that advice asked for.

data_cna_hg19.seg holds segments for the 646 tissue samples only (no plasma sample), so it cannot rescue copy-number actionability in plasma; team B checked ID overlap, neither needed it. Patient-table treatment fields (CRDB_PRIOR_RX, CRDB_NOSYSTXT) are sparsely filled and were not used.

MSI_TYPE is blank and MSI_SCORE is -1 for all 800 plasma samples (MSI not assessed in plasma), and plasma TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS is a count on a 129-gene panel; any tier that counts MSI-H or TMB>=10 as a biomarker is not comparable between plasma and tissue.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A: 'the rule table is my own approximation ... SV fusion calls were classified from Event_Info text' - reported, not resolved. The sensitivity runs removed DNA-repair genes and unmatched samples only; there is no leave-one-rule-out table and no check of SV rows against the frame/region columns.
Team A: 'a much narrower definition (e.g. non-lung only, or excluding EGFR/FGFR3) could approach 20%' - stated, but the narrowest defensible definition was not computed with a CI.

Team B: 'did not verify individual variant calls (e.g. MET exon 14 splice positions, which HRR truncations count as oncogenic)' and 'uncertain by roughly +/-10 points' - reported, not resolved. The narrow-definition stress tests (24-31%) were given without patient-cluster CIs, so it is not shown that the lowest of them excludes 20%.

Team B: 'a reader who holds that actionability must come from a column in the data could argue for Not verifiable' - named, argued in one sentence, not tested. Team B also received no passed-down pitfalls and does not report filtering Mutation_Status UNKNOWN rows or unmatched samples.
second_readings: 'the samples' = the plasma cfDNA samples only (the study's new assay), the tissue samples, all 1,446, or one sample per patient. Both teams stratified; the verdict is the same in each stratum they report.

'20%' as an exact point value (both teams' reading) versus 'about 20%' with a tolerance versus 'at least 20%'. Under an 'at least' reading the teams' own figures would support rather than contradict the claim; the task says the hypothesis is a definite claim, so the point reading is the more natural one, but neither team said why it rejected the other.

'clinically actionable' = standard-of-care biomarker in that tumour type only, or any knowledgebase level including investigational, off-tumour-type and resistance markers, and as of the study's date or as of today. The fraction moves from about a third to about three quarters across these readings.

'samples with somatic alterations' = any released call of any kind (both teams) versus samples with a tumour-derived protein-altering alteration (excluding promoter/intronic-only, intergenic SVs, possible clonal-haematopoiesis calls).

Label reading: with no actionability variable in any table, 'Not verifiable' is a possible label under a strict reading of the task; both teams chose 'False' because the inputs to an annotation (gene, protein change, CNA, fusion, tumour type) are present.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed label 'False' fairly well but not fully: two independently written rule tables both put every stratum well above 20% with cluster CIs that exclude it, yet the same tables disagree with each other by about ten points on the same samples, neither was checked against a reference annotation or an era-matched definition, and the narrowest stress tests (22-25%) were reported without CIs. The remaining risk is less that the fraction is really 20% than that the label depends on a definition the data do not contain, which the teams named but did not close.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: A second, independently written rule table applied to the same altered plasma samples puts roughly 60 samples in a different strict-tier class than yours, so the two tables do not measure the same thing. Print a per-rule table for your strict tier in plasma: for each rule (gene x alteration x tumour type) the number of altered ACCESS129 samples it flags and the number that are actionable through that rule alone. Then recompute the strict plasma fraction with each rule removed one at a time, and with all rules removed that a careful annotator could dispute (somatic DNA-repair genes, resistance mutations, rules resting on a splice or SV interpretation). Give the patient-cluster CI of the lowest result. Does any of these put 20% inside the CI, and if so does that change your label or your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You marked 'knowledgebase era' as checked, but no era-matched tier appears in your results. Mark each rule in your strict tier as standard of care already at the time these samples were sequenced (the panel versions date them) or only later, and recompute the strict fraction for plasma using the earlier set only: all altered samples, and first plasma sample per patient, each with a patient-cluster CI. State before you look what distance from 20% you would call agreement. Does the era-matched figure change the label, and do you regard that definition as a defensible reading of 'clinically actionable' or not, and why?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: The 800 plasma samples are split by columns you did not use: SAMPLE_TYPE (Unknown 525 / Primary 156 / Metastasis 118), TUMOR_PURITY (blank 582 / 'default' 216), the sample order within patient (506 patients with one plasma sample, 111 with 2-14), and whether the patient also has a tissue sample (449 of 617). Tabulate the altered-sample count and your strict actionable fraction within each level of these four splits. Is any split associated with a large difference, does any sizeable stratum have a CI that includes 20%, and does that tell you that 'the samples' might be a sub-cohort rather than all 800?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your weakest point names SV calls classified from Event_Info text. Plasma has 72 SV rows in 70 samples, many labelled intergenic, 'Antisense Fusion' or 'Deletion of N exons'. List every SV row that makes a sample strict-tier actionable, with Site1/Site2 gene, region, Site2_Effect_On_Frame, Class and Annotation, and count how many samples are actionable through an SV alone. For patients who also have a tissue sample, count how many of the plasma alterations your strict tier relies on (mutations and SVs) are also present in that patient's tissue. Recompute the strict plasma fraction with SV-only actionable samples removed. Does either check move the result relative to 20%?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: A second, independently written rule table applied to the same altered cfDNA samples puts roughly 60 samples in a different strict-tier class than yours, so the two tables do not measure the same thing, and you state you did not verify MET exon 14 splice positions or which DNA-repair truncations count. Print a per-rule table for your strict tier in cfDNA: for each rule (gene x alteration x tumour type) the number of altered samples it flags and the number actionable through that rule alone. List the actual MET and DNA-repair-gene calls (HGVSp_Short, HGVSc, Variant_Classification, cancer type) your strict tier counts. Recompute the strict fraction with each rule removed one at a time and with all unverified or disputable rules removed together. Does the lowest result still exclude 20%, and does the exercise change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your narrow-definition stress tests give 24-31% and your leave-NSCLC-out strict figure is 25.4%, but none of these carries a patient-cluster CI, and one definition falls below 20%. For each stress-test definition, and for a strict tier restricted to biomarkers that were already standard of care when these samples were sequenced (the panel versions date them), report the fraction among altered cfDNA samples and among first cfDNA sample per patient, each with a patient-cluster bootstrap CI. State before you look what distance from 20% you would call agreement. Which of these definitions do you hold to be defensible readings of 'clinically actionable', and does any defensible one have a CI that includes 20%? If so, does the label change?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your notes do not say that non-somatic or doubtful calls were removed. Tabulate Mutation_Status in data_mutations.txt (38 rows are UNKNOWN), SOMATIC_STATUS in the sample table (6 Unmatched, 1 of them cfDNA) and the Event_Info / Site2_Effect_On_Frame / Class of the 72 cfDNA SV rows (many are intergenic, antisense or intragenic deletions). Recompute numerator and denominator for cfDNA keeping only SOMATIC rows, excluding unmatched samples, counting an SV as actionable only when the frame and gene columns support a functional fusion, and treating DNA-repair-gene hits in plasma (possible clonal haematopoiesis or germline) as a separate tier. How many samples leave the denominator and the numerator, and does the strict fraction move relative to 20%?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: The 800 cfDNA samples are split by columns you did not use: SAMPLE_TYPE (Unknown 525 / Primary 156 / Metastasis 118), TUMOR_PURITY (blank 582 / 'default' 216), the sample order within patient (506 patients with one cfDNA sample, 111 with 2-14), and whether the patient also has a tissue sample (449 of 617). Tabulate the altered-sample count and your strict actionable fraction within each level of these four splits, and for patients with both sample classes count how many of the cfDNA alterations your strict tier relies on are also present in that patient's tissue. Is any split associated with a large difference, does any sizeable stratum have a CI that includes 20%, and does that change which samples you take 'the samples' to be?

In the OncoKB knowledge base, how are the therapeutic levels of evidence (1, 2, 3A, 3B, 4, R1, R2) defined, which of them do published tumour-sequencing and liquid-biopsy studies conventionally include when they report the share of samples with 'clinically actionable' alterations, and how is a sample's highest level assigned when its alteration is standard of care only in a different tumour type?
questions.why: Both teams built their own tiers and their strict tiers disagree by about ten percentage points on the same samples; knowing which levels the phrase conventionally covers tells them which of their tiers is the one to compare with the claim.

questions.question: Which gene-alteration and tumour-type pairs are OncoKB level 1 or level 2, and in which year did each reach that level (in particular KRAS G12C and MET exon 14 skipping and RET fusions in lung cancer, PIK3CA in breast cancer, FGFR3 in bladder cancer, IDH1 and FGFR2 fusions in cholangiocarcinoma, BRAF V600E outside melanoma, ERBB2 amplification and mutations)?
questions.why: Neither team computed an era-matched tier; a dated list lets each team mark which of its rules were standard of care when the samples were sequenced and test whether the conclusion depends on later approvals.

questions.question: For somatic (not germline) mutations in homologous-recombination repair genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2 and PALB2, in which tumour types does OncoKB assign level 1 or 2, does it require the variant to be truncating or otherwise known oncogenic, and which MET splice-site or intronic positions are annotated as exon 14 skipping?
questions.why: One team named exactly these two rule families as unverified and the other treated DNA-repair genes as a sensitivity tier; they are the most likely source of the gap between the two strict tiers.

findings.question: In the OncoKB knowledge base, how are the therapeutic levels of evidence (1, 2, 3A, 3B, 4, R1, R2) defined, which of them do published tumour-sequencing and liquid-biopsy studies conventionally include when they report the share of samples with 'clinically actionable' alterations, and how is a sample's highest level assigned when its alteration is standard of care only in a different tumour type?
findings.answer: DEFINITIONS. Level 1 = FDA-recognized biomarker predictive of response to an FDA-approved drug in this indication (tumour type). Level 2 = standard-care biomarker recommended by the NCCN or other expert panels, predictive of response to an FDA-approved drug in this indication (called 2A before Dec 2019). Level 3A = compelling clinical evidence supports the biomarker as predictive of response to a drug in this indication (not yet standard care). Level 3B = standard-care or investigational biomarker predictive of response to an FDA-approved or investigational drug in ANOTHER indication (since Dec 2019 this merges the old 2B and 3B). Level 4 = compelling biological (laboratory) evidence only. R1 = standard-care biomarker predictive of resistance to an FDA-approved drug in this indication (e.g. EGFR T790M, RAS in colorectal). R2 = compelling clinical evidence of resistance (investigational). OncoKB groups 1 and 2 as 'standard care', 3A/3B as 'clinical evidence' and 4 as 'biological evidence'. Exact current wording for 1, 3A, 4, R1, R2 could not be read from the OncoKB levels page (it is an image); those definitions are from the 2017 OncoKB paper and the page's short labels, while the wording for 2 and 3B is verbatim from the OncoKB annotator README. CONVENTION. There is no single convention; the web does not settle one tier. What published studies did: (a) levels 1-2 only ('standard care' / 'clinically actionable' in the MSK clinical update: 'harboring an OncoKB Level 1 or Level 2 predictive biomarker'): 7.5% of samples in the 2017 OncoKB paper, 8.9% (2017 knowledge base) rising to 31.6% (2022 knowledge base) of 47,271 tumours in the 2023 OncoKB paper; (b) levels 1-3A ('at least one clinically actionable genomic alteration (OncoKB levels 1-3A)' in the 2023 OncoKB paper, which calls 3B, 4 and no-level 'limited to no clinical actionability'): 18.1% (2017) to 35.9% (2022); (c) levels 1-3B (the usual headline in 2017-2022 cohort papers): 36.7% of patients in the MSK-IMPACT 10,000-patient paper, 41% in the 2017 OncoKB paper, 44% in a 1,671-patient biliary cfDNA study (which separately called levels 1 and 3A in that tumour 'clinically significant'), 48% in an ASCO 2022 abstract ('OncoKB Levels 1/2/3'); (d) levels 1-4 called 'potentially actionable' in a 2019 liquid-biopsy abstract. Level 4 is usually left out of the headline and R1/R2 are resistance levels that are not counted as actionable-for-response. Studies level only alterations that OncoKB calls oncogenic or likely oncogenic. So the teams should report 1-2, 1-3A and 1-3B separately; a claim worded 'clinically actionable' in a 2017-2022 sequencing paper most often means 1-3B, and one worded 'standard care' or 'FDA-recognized/guideline' means 1-2. CROSS-TUMOUR RULE. A level 1, 2 or 3A biomarker does NOT keep its level in another tumour type: it is assigned Level 3B there (Level 2B in the pre-Dec-2019 scheme). Propagation is solid-to-solid or heme-to-heme only; R1/R2 and Level 4 never propagate, and some lineage-specific and all germline associations do not propagate. Exceptions are tumour-agnostic approvals (e.g. MSI-H, NTRK fusions, TMB-H, RET fusions, BRAF V600E since 2022), which are Level 1 in all solid tumours. A sample takes the single highest level among all its alterations; the annotator's order is R1 > 1 > 2 > 3A > 3B > 4 > R2 (HIGHEST_LEVEL) and 1 > 2 > 3A > 3B > 4 for the sensitive-only column (HIGHEST_SENSITIVE_LEVEL), which is the one to use for an actionability share. NOTE: one search hit looked like the study behind the task's dataset; it was not opened and nothing here comes from it. CONFIDENCE DETAIL: high for the definitions and the Level 3B cross-tumour rule; medium for the convention, because published studies use 1-2, 1-3A, 1-3B or 1-4 and the web does not settle a single one.

findings.question: Which gene-alteration and tumour-type pairs are OncoKB level 1 or level 2, and in which year did each reach that level (in particular KRAS G12C and MET exon 14 skipping and RET fusions in lung cancer, PIK3CA in breast cancer, FGFR3 in bladder cancer, IDH1 and FGFR2 fusions in cholangiocarcinoma, BRAF V600E outside melanoma, ERBB2 amplification and mutations)?
findings.answer: Year each pair reached Level 1 or 2 in OncoKB (from the dated OncoKB news log, the 2017 and 2023 OncoKB papers and the current actionable-genes table). KRAS G12C, lung (NSCLC): Level 3A Dec 2019; Level 1 June 2021 (sotorasib), adagrasib Level 1 Dec 2022. KRAS G12C colorectal: 3A Nov 2021, Level 2 by 2024, Level 1 by Jan 2025; pancreatic Level 2 May 2023. MET exon 14 skipping, NSCLC: Level 2A already in 2017 (crizotinib, NCCN); Level 1 May 2020 (capmatinib), tepotinib Mar 2021. MET amplification NSCLC is Level 2 today. RET fusions, NSCLC: Level 2 before 2020 (cabozantinib/vandetanib; selpercatinib and pralsetinib added at Level 2 Nov-Dec 2018); Level 1 May 2020 (selpercatinib), pralsetinib Sep 2020; thyroid Level 1 2020; all solid tumours Level 1 Oct 2022. PIK3CA, breast: Level 3A in 2017; Level 1 June 2019 (alpelisib). By Oct 2022 Level 1 is limited to C420R, E542K, E545A/D/G/K, Q546E/R, H1047L/R/Y and other oncogenic PIK3CA mutations are Level 2; capivasertib Level 1 Dec 2023. FGFR3, bladder: Level 3 in 2017; Level 1 May 2019 (erdafitinib; R248C, S249C, G370C, Y373C and FGFR3 fusions); other oncogenic FGFR3 mutations in bladder are Level 2 today. IDH1 (R132C/G/H/L/S), cholangiocarcinoma: 2B to 3A Dec 2019; Level 1 Aug 2021 (ivosidenib). IDH1/IDH2 in AML were Level 1 from 2017-2018. FGFR2 fusions, cholangiocarcinoma: Level 3 in 2017; Level 1 May 2020 (pemigatinib). BRAF V600E outside melanoma (melanoma Level 1 since 2011): NSCLC Level 2A in early 2017 then Level 1 in 2017; anaplastic thyroid Level 1 2018; Erdheim-Chester/histiocytosis Level 1 2017-2018; colorectal Level 1 Apr 2020 (encorafenib + cetuximab); glioma Level 2 May 2020; biliary Level 2 June 2022; all solid tumours except colorectal Level 1 Sep 2022. ERBB2 amplification: breast Level 1 (1998), oesophagogastric Level 1 (2010); colorectal Level 2 Apr 2020 and Level 1 today (the date of the step up was not read; the FDA approval was in 2023); biliary, salivary, uterine serous and small bowel Level 2 in 2024; other solid tumours 3A since May 2024. ERBB2 mutations: NSCLC Level 2A Dec 2019 (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), Level 1 Sep 2022 (trastuzumab deruxtecan); breast was 3A in 2017 and is Level 2 today (the date was not read); elsewhere 3B. Other Level 1 pairs and the year the biomarker was first FDA-recognized: EGFR L858R/exon 19 deletion NSCLC (2013 label), EGFR T790M (2015), EGFR S768I/L861Q/G719X (2018), EGFR exon 20 insertions (2021), ALK fusions NSCLC (2011), ROS1 fusions NSCLC (2016), KIT in GIST (2002), PDGFRA exon 18 GIST (2020), BRCA1/2 ovarian (2014; somatic 2018), HRR genes in prostate (2020), MSI-H all solid tumours (2017), NTRK fusions all solid tumours (2018), TMB-H all solid tumours (2020). Scale: 14 genes in 12 cancer types were Level 1 in March 2017; 45 genes plus MSI-H and TMB-H by Oct 2022. Samples at Level 1-2 rose from 8.9% under the 2017 knowledge base to 31.6% under the 2022 one in the same 47,271 tumours, so the knowledge-base version alone can move a strict tier by far more than 10 points. For a cohort sequenced around 2019-2021, an era-matched Level 1-2 tier would exclude KRAS G12C (before mid-2021), IDH1 cholangiocarcinoma (before Aug 2021), ERBB2-mutant NSCLC at Level 1 (before Sep 2022), tumour-agnostic BRAF V600E and RET fusions (before Sep/Oct 2022), and TMB-H before 2020. This list is not exhaustive: the full Level 2 list (about 750 table rows) was parsed from a page whose level column was lost in extraction, so level blocks were inferred and cross-checked against the dated news entries. CONFIDENCE DETAIL: high for the dated pairs named in the question; medium for completeness of the wider Level 2 list and for the two dates marked as not read.

findings.question: For somatic (not germline) mutations in homologous-recombination repair genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2 and PALB2, in which tumour types does OncoKB assign level 1 or 2, does it require the variant to be truncating or otherwise known oncogenic, and which MET splice-site or intronic positions are annotated as exon 14 skipping?
findings.answer: TUMOUR TYPES (somatic 'Oncogenic Mutations', current OncoKB). BRCA1 and BRCA2: Level 1 in ovarian/fallopian tube/peritoneal cancer (olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib, olaparib + bevacizumab) and in prostate cancer (olaparib, rucaparib, and PARP inhibitor combinations); Level 2 in pancreatic adenocarcinoma/acinar cell carcinoma (rucaparib, since Mar 2022) and BRCA2 in uterine sarcoma (Mar 2022). Somatic BRCA1/2 in breast cancer is Level 3A, not 1 or 2: it was Level 2 from Dec 2018 and was demoted to 3A in Nov 2021 because the FDA labels are germline-only; somatic BRCA1/2 with olaparib in pancreatic cancer is also 3A. ATM, CHEK2, PALB2 (and BARD1, BRIP1, CDK12, CHEK1, FANCL, RAD51B, RAD51C, RAD51D, RAD54L): Level 1 in prostate cancer only (olaparib, since June 2020; talazoparib + enzalutamide added 2023). PALB2 is also Level 2 in pancreatic cancer (rucaparib, Mar 2022). In every other solid tumour type these genes reach only Level 3B by propagation. Before June 2020 ATM was Level 4 and the non-BRCA HRR genes had no Level 1-2 anywhere. The CHEK2 page was read and shows prostate only; the ATM gene page failed to load, so ATM rests on the actionable-genes table and news log. ONCOGENIC REQUIREMENT. Yes. The level attaches to 'Oncogenic Mutations', defined by OncoKB as point mutations, rearrangements/fusions or gene deletions 'considered oncogenic, likely oncogenic or resistance'; variants of unknown significance get no level. The variant need not be truncating, but for tumour suppressors OncoKB curates all truncating mutations (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site) as likely oncogenic, so in practice: truncating variants and deep deletions count; missense or in-frame variants count only if individually curated as oncogenic or likely oncogenic; amplification does not count. A biliary cfDNA study applying this rule found about 90% of BRCA1/2 cfDNA variants unclassified. A team that counts every HRR-gene mutation, or counts them outside ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer, will overstate the Level 1-2 tier. MET EXON 14. OncoKB's levelled group in NSCLC is 'D1010, Exon 14 Deletion, Exon 14 in-frame deletions (963_1010del), Exon 14 splice mutations (963_1010splice)': Level 1 capmatinib and tepotinib, Level 2 crizotinib. Individually listed variants include X963_splice (acceptor end of exon 14), X1006_splice to X1010_splice (donor end), D1010 and D1010H/N/Y; all are likely oncogenic. Y1003 substitutions (CBL binding site) are Level 3A, not 1 or 2. Some files use the alternative isoform numbering 981_1028 for the same exon. OncoKB matches on gene, protein change and consequence, not on genomic coordinates. Its SOP defines a splice mutation as a change in the 2-base region at either end of an intron and leaves variant-type assignment to the sequencing assay. The annotator maps the mutation-file class Splice_Site to splice_region_variant and has no mapping for Intron or Splice_Region. So a deeper intronic variant (polypyrimidine tract or branch point) is annotated as exon 14 skipping only if the mutation file already labels it as a splice variant at codons 963-1010 (e.g. X963_splice, X1010_splice) or as an exon 14 in-frame deletion. The web did not settle an explicit list of intronic genomic positions: no source read gives one. CONFIDENCE DETAIL: high for tumour types and the oncogenic requirement; low for intronic positions, which the web did not settle beyond the protein-level splice variants.
